newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivorian cocoa yields may offset loss from eviction.
newsitem.headline: Ivorian cocoa yields may offset loss from eviction.

text.p: The effect on cocoa volumes of Ivory Coast's policy of evicting farmers from illegal forest encampments could be offset by better husbandry and replanting elsewhere, donor sources say.
Ivorian forestry officials last week told Reuters they had given migrant farmers until August to quit their illegal encampments or be burnt out in line with government policy set in March.

"Yields per hectare are low in the forests," one donor source told Reuters. "Output could be raised elsewhere to match lost production simply with better husbandry and without clearing for new farms. We will support that."

Ivory Coast, the world's largest cocoa producer, had a record 1.2 million tonnes crop in its 1995/96 season (Oct-Sept) and is not far behind in 1996/97. The 1997/98 crop is also showing signs of large potential harvests, crop analysts say.
In March, the government threw its weight behind a European Union-backed 1996-2005 reforestation plan.
It said 30 percent of protected forests was "illegally occupied" by up to 450,000 farmers and their relatives, growing up to 100,000 tonnes of cocoa.
The forests came under protection following a 1973 law. Farmers settling after that date are mostly viewed by officials as illegal.

Evicted farmers building shanty shacks at the edge of forests told Reuters last week they had been allowed to carry on harvesting cocoa but would not be allowed to live in the forest, or chop down more trees. That would make husbandry difficult.
Cocoa trees thrive in forest areas but need occasional trimming and maintenance to ensure long-term yields.

Illegal cocoa production in protected forests has accelerated in recent years but forest cover has fallen to around 3.9 million hectares from 12 million hectares before independence from France in 1960. Illegal logging has also contributed to the decline.

Industry analysts and cocoa buyers expect no effect on overall Ivorian cocoa production for 3-5 years although the total number of hectares being illegally farmed is unknown, as is the annual output of cocoa and coffee.
Estimates of 50,000 tonnes by some crop analysts are at variance with government estimates of 100,000 tonnes or more.
Tropical forest species seedlings for replanting have been positioned around forest areas by the state agency, Societe De Developpement des Forets (SODEFOR).

In March, the Ivory Coast discussed with donors guidelines for clarifying land tenancy laws which have become blurred since post-independence president Felix Houphouet-Boigny said farmers would be the owners of land they planted.
"Since then there have been farmers installed by some political authorities and then normal migrants who are more obviously illegal," said one donor.
Some industry analysts say the policy might stop in midstream because of land rights disputes, a lack of funds, and enforcement difficulties.
